content: The CD81 molecule, also referred to as CD81 (Cluster of Differentiation 81), is a protein encoded by the CD81 gene in humans. It is also known by other names, including the 26 kDa cell surface protein, TAPA-1 (Target of the Antiproliferative Antibody 1), and Tetraspanin-28 (Tspan-28). This protein does not undergo post-translational modifications and is characterized by the presence of four transmembrane domains. Both the N-terminus and C-terminus of the protein are located on the intracellular side of the membrane. The CD81 gene is expressed in hematopoietic, endothelial, and epithelial cells, but it is absent in erythrocytes, platelets, and neutrophils. The protein encoded by the CD81 gene belongs to the transmembrane 4 superfamily, also known as the tetraspanin family. Members of this family are cell-surface proteins that are defined by the presence of four hydrophobic domains. These proteins are involved in signal transduction processes that regulate cell development, activation, growth, and motility. CD81 is a cell surface glycoprotein that forms complexes with integrins. It has been shown to promote muscle cell fusion and support the maintenance of myotubes. Additionally, it may play a role in signal transduction. The CD81 gene is located in a tumor-suppressor gene region, making it a candidate gene for malignancies. Other members of the tetraspanin family include CD9, CD37, CD53, CD63, CD82, and CD151. CD81 interacts directly with members of the immunoglobulin superfamily, such as IGSF8 (CD316) and CD36. On the surface of B cells, it forms a signal transduction complex with CD19, CD21, and Leu-13 (CD225). On T cells, CD81 associates with CD4 and CD8 and provides a costimulatory signal in conjunction with CD3. Clinically, CD81 plays a critical role in the attachment and/or entry of Hepatitis C virus (HCV) into cells by interacting with the virus's E1/E2 glycoprotein heterodimer. The large extracellular loop (LEL) of CD81 binds to the hepatitis E2 glycoprotein dimer with high affinity. However, only 30% of HCV-E2-engaged CD81 is internalized after 12 hours, suggesting that CD81 primarily functions as an attachment receptor for HCV. CD81 also appears to be involved in liver invasion by Plasmodium species. It is required for the entry of Plasmodium vivax sporozoites into human hepatocytes and Plasmodium yoelii sporozoites into murine hepatocytes. In the context of HIV, CD81 is utilized by HIV Gag proteins as part of tetraspanin-enriched microdomains (containing at least CD81, CD82, and CD63) to serve as a platform for virion assembly and release. Purified HIV produced by MOLT/HIV cells contains CD81. Anti-CD81 antibodies reduce HIV production threefold, although CD81-free virus is more infectious. Engagement of CD81 lowers the signaling threshold required to trigger T-cell/CD3-mediated proviral DNA synthesis in CD4+ T cells. CD81 also appears to play a role in the pathogenesis of influenza. CD81 has been shown to interact with several proteins, including TSPAN4, CD19, CD9, PTGFRN, CD117, and CD29. Additionally, ligands such as benzyl salicylate and terfenadine have been demonstrated to bind to CD81.
